method: Blind expert labelling, extending v1 from 3 functions to 10. Every function added here was read from source and labelled BEFORE any scorer was run against it, and the file was written to disk before measurement. v1's three functions are carried over unchanged so the two versions are comparable. Functions were chosen to widen the shape of the corpus, not to favour any scorer: v1 was three behaviour-dense functions with almost no plumbing, which gave the tier partition nothing to separate. v2 deliberately includes a thin wrapper (shlex.split), a validation-dominated parse (ipaddress._ip_int_from_string), a flat if-chain with no loop (urllib.parse.urlsplit), a function containing a near-duplicate of itself (bisect.bisect_right), and three functions containing genuine plumbing lines - bound-method bindings and invariant assertions - which are the sharpest test in the corpus. v3 adds six more functions, labelled the same way - read from source and recorded before any scorer was run on them: a pure string algorithm with a large constant-aliasing preamble (posixpath.normpath), a small filter-and-rank (difflib.get_close_matches), an early-return case analysis (urllib.parse.urljoin), a validation-heavy dual-algorithm method (random.Random.sample), a two-branch numeric routine (statistics.quantiles) and a recursive dispatch loop (string.Formatter._vformat). Under the project's revised objective the rater's judgement is the explicit target of approximation, not a proxy for something else, so single-rater is no longer listed as a bias for this file's primary use.
importance_scale: 10 = changing this line materially changes what the function does or returns; 5 = supporting work that a reader must follow but that carries no decision; 0 = removable with no behavioural consequence (logging, debug, pure micro-optimisation).
known_biases: Single rater, no inter-rater agreement, and the rater implemented the tool under test.

Labels are for a *reader's* sense of importance, which is not identical to 'a mutant here would be killed'. Mutation testing would disagree in places, especially on error-handling paths that tests rarely cover.
Three functions is a small sample. Treat rank correlation from it as directional, not conclusive.
Python only. JVM lowering could behave differently.

Still a single rater, and still the person who designed the incumbent scorer's feature set. Extra labelling adds statistical power but does not remove that confound; see eval/mutation_oracle.py for an oracle that does not run through anyone's judgement.
primary_metric: Spearman rank correlation between these importances and each scorer's per-line score, computed per function then averaged. Rank correlation rather than tier agreement, because all three functions are almost entirely behaviour-carrying — well-written stdlib code genuinely has little plumbing, so a tier partition has little to separate. The useful question is whether a scorer ORDERS lines the way a reader would.
